stem: After a lumbar puncture, a client develops a bilateral headache that becomes markedly worse when sitting or standing and improves when lying supine. Which complication should the nurse suspect?
rationale: Postdural puncture headache is a recognized complication of lumbar puncture caused by cerebrospinal fluid leakage and intracranial hypotension. A characteristic feature is a headache that worsens in the upright position and improves when supine. The positional pattern described is not characteristic of a local puncture-site infection, hypoglycemia, or hypertensive emergency.
educational_objective: Recognize a new postural headache after lumbar puncture—worse upright and improved supine—as a characteristic presentation of postdural puncture headache.
source_organization: National Library of Medicine / NCBI Bookshelf — StatPearls
source_version_date: Last updated February 15, 2025; StatPearls 2026 edition; accessed 2026-08-17
source_locator: Introduction; History and Physical; Deterrence and Patient Education — PDPH follows CSF leakage after dural puncture, is worse upright and improves supine, and routine bed rest after lumbar puncture is not supported as prevention
source_claim_supported: PDPH is a lumbar-puncture complication from CSF leakage/intracranial hypotension with a characteristic orthostatic headache; evidence does not support routine post-lumbar-puncture bed rest to prevent PDPH.
blueprint_locator: Reduction of Risk Potential, Appendix A printed pp.43-45 / PDF pp.46-48: assess for abnormal response following a diagnostic test/procedure; evaluate client responses to procedures and treatments; System-Specific Assessments
